## 1. Grammar and morphology

The verse opens with the vocative yā ayyuhā lladhīna āmanū — "O you who have believed" — where ayyuhā is tagged nominative as the head of the vocative construction, lladhīna is a masculine plural relative clause, and āmanū is Form IV perfect, third masculine plural, with no object expressed. The addressee is defined by prior belief, not by the content of the command that follows.

The prohibition is carried by lā + jussive: lā taʾkulū ("do not eat/consume"), Form I imperfect, second masculine plural, mood jussive — a negative command, not a statement about habitual conduct. The object is al-ribā, tagged accusative, definite, from the root ر-ب-و. The verb akala with a definite object of consumption is the standard Qurʾānic frame for consuming wealth illicitly (compare 4:29, 2:188).

Two accusative modifiers follow: aḍʿāfan (masculine plural, indefinite, from ض-ع-ف) and muḍāʿafah (feminine singular, indefinite, from the same root). The plural–singular mismatch is grammatically regular: a distributive or intensifying construction where the feminine singular adjective qualifies the plural noun distributively — "doubled, each doubling multiplied" — an escalation pattern, not a simple apposition. The same root supplies both the noun and the participle, so the phrase is internally cohesive: doubling upon doubling.

The command resumes with wa-ttaqū ("and be mindful of"), Form VIII imperative, second masculine plural, taking Allāh as its accusative object. The particle laʿalla + tufliḥūna ("that you may prosper") closes the verse: tufliḥūna is Form IV imperfect, second masculine plural, indicative. Laʿalla here expresses attainable hope contingent on compliance, a recurring Qurʾānic collocation with ittaqū.

No conditional particle, exception, or scope-limiting qualifier appears anywhere in the verse. The prohibition attaches to al-ribā itself; aḍʿāfan muḍāʿafah is an accusative description of the ribā being consumed, not a restrictive clause narrowing the prohibition to a subset of ribā. Nothing in the morphology licenses reading "doubled and multiplied" as a boundary marker distinguishing prohibited from permissible ribā.

## 2. Verse proximity analysis

The verse sits within a sustained address to the believers following the Badr narrative (3:123–129). The preceding verses establish divine control over victory, forgiveness, and punishment — "to God belongs what is in the heavens and the earth" (3:129) — before the address turns to economic conduct. The sequence is not accidental: 3:130 prohibits consuming ribā, 3:131 commands mindfulness of the Fire prepared for the disbelievers, and 3:132 commands obedience to God and the Messenger "that you may be shown mercy." The three verses form a single exhortatory block moving from specific prohibition to general eschatological warning to obedience, each closing with a purpose clause (laʿallakum tufliḥūna, laʿallakum turḥamūna implied by context).

The following verses (3:133–134) urge hastening toward forgiveness and a paradise "prepared for the muttaqīn," defined as those who spend in ease and hardship, restrain anger, and pardon people. This immediately contextualizes the ribā prohibition within a broader economic ethic: the same believers forbidden to consume ribā are commanded to give, forgive, and pardon — the inverse economic posture. The contrast between consuming (akala) and giving (yunfiqūna) is the structural logic of the passage.

The prohibition's placement after 3:123 ("fattaqū llāha laʿallakum tashkurūna") and before 3:131 ("fattaqū l-nāra") shows the taqwā formula framing both gratitude and fear. Within this frame, ribā consumption is presented as conduct incompatible with the prosperity (falāḥ) that the passage promises the obedient. The doubling language of 3:130 gains resonance from the surrounding divine arithmetic: God multiplies charity (2:245, 2:265) while obliterating ribā (2:276) — increase belongs to God's economy, not to extraction from debtors.

## 3. Pan-textual evidence

The ribā cluster in Sūrat al-Baqara supplies the doctrinal frame for 3:130. At 2:275, those who consume ribā are contrasted with those who trade: their claim that "trade is like ribā" is answered by the divine distinction — "God has made trade lawful and forbidden ribā." The verse pairs the consumption verb (yaʾkulūna) with the same accusative object (al-ribā) found in 3:130, confirming that the prohibition targets the act of consuming the increase, not merely its extreme forms. 2:276 states the divine economy directly: "God obliterates ribā and causes charity to grow (yurbī l-ṣadaqāt)" — the root ر-ب-و appears in both halves, one increase voided, the other nurtured. 2:278 commands abandoning "what remains of ribā," and 2:279 fixes the boundary: repentant creditors retain "your principal sums" (ruʾūs amwālikum), "wronging no one and being wronged by no one." The principal-only rule is stated without gradation; no verse in the cluster introduces a permissible surplus threshold.

The doubling vocabulary of 3:130 has its own pan-textual profile. At 2:245, God "multiplies it for him many multiples (aḍʿāfan kathīrah)" for the goodly loan; at 2:265, the garden on a rabbah (high ground) yields "its produce doubled (ḍiʿfayn)." The root ض-ع-ف in these passages describes multiplication as divine recompense, not as a legal category. 3:130's aḍʿāfan muḍāʿafah thus borrows the language of multiplication and applies it to what humans extract — a pointed inversion: doubling belongs to God's giving, and when it appears on the side of consumption from debtors, it is forbidden.

30:39 sharpens the definitional question: "What you give in ribā that it may increase in people's wealth does not increase with God; what you give in zakāh seeking God's face — those are the multipliers (humu l-muḍʿifūn)." The verse names ribā as a category of giving intended to grow the principal, and denies it divine increase, while assigning the true multiplication to charity. The participle muḍʿifūn shares the doubling root of 3:130, reinforcing that multiplication language in the Qurʾān consistently tracks increase-seeking conduct, whether condemned (ribā) or commended (charity).

4:161 extends the prohibition backward: "their taking ribā though they were forbidden it" — a past community's violation, with no indication that the forbidden portion was limited to excessive rates. The root ر-ب-و elsewhere carries growth and swelling (13:17, the froth rābiyan; 22:5, the earth swells and grows), confirming the lexical core of increase while leaving the ribā prohibition anchored in the specific legal cluster.

The falāḥ collocation frames the verse's close. Laʿallakum tufliḥūna follows ittaqū llāha at 2:189, 3:200, 5:35, 5:100, 8:45, 22:77, 62:10 — always as the purpose of a commanded conduct. Its negative counterpart recurs: "the wrongdoers will not prosper" (6:21, 6:135, 28:37), "the fabricators against God will not prosper" (10:69, 16:116). 3:130 thus places ribā consumption on the non-prospering side of a Qurʾān-wide binary, with 23:1 and 91:9 defining the prospering side as belief and purification.

Evidence limits: the ribā cluster (2:275–279, 3:130, 4:161, 30:39) was examined in full; the doubling-root occurrences at 7:38, 17:75, 33:30, 33:68, 34:37, 38:61 were not supplied and remain unexamined. No supplied verse presents a rate threshold or a permitted category of ribā.

## 4. Qurʾān-centric research angles

- **Ribā as any increase over principal, established by root semantics.** The Architecture of Debt-Money and Interest surveys the twenty occurrences of ر-ب-و (surplus at 2:275–278, 3:130, 4:161, 30:39; swelling at 13:17, 22:5; high ground at 2:265, 23:50; bringing up at 17:24, 26:18; exceeding at 16:92, 69:10) and argues the root consistently denotes increase, so ribā covers any surplus, not only compound interest.

- **"Doubled and multiplied" as descriptive, not definitional.** The same work reads 3:130's aḍʿāfan muḍāʿafah as historically illustrative of what people were doing, arguing that 2:279's principal-only rule supplies the legal definition; a low rate compounding to multiples of principal would collapse the distinction, and reading 3:130 as permitting small ribā would create a contradiction (tested against 4:82's non-duality principle).

- **Universal, non-dualistic prohibition.** The work contrasts the Qurʾān's categorical ban (2:275–279, 3:130, 4:161, 30:39) with in-group/out-group distinctions in the Pentateuch and with later legal fictions (heter iska, lucrum cessans, murābaḥa markups), arguing the latter equal principal plus a time-based premium.

- **Global debt as structural ribā.** The work argues that money created as principal only while debt carries interest forces perpetual expansion, reading 3:130's doubling language as describing a system-level compounding dynamic rather than a single transaction.

- **Gerrans's terminological frame.** Sam Gerrans renders alladhīna āmanū as "those who heed warning" (defined via 2:257 against 2:6) and glosses 3:130's prohibition as usury — "the payment of rent for money or goods" — treating the verse as one of the sins listed in his Muḥammad chapter, with 2:278–279 as the war-declaration boundary.

## 5. Further reading

claims.claim: The root ر-ب-و consistently means increase, addition, surplus, growth, or swelling across all its Qurʾānic usages, so ribā denotes any increase over principal.
claims.source: What is Ribā in the Qurʾān?
premises: 20 occurrences of the root surveyed across senses: surplus, swelling, high ground, bringing up, exceeding
All usages share the core sense of rise, increase, or addition
Ribā in 2:275–278, 3:130, 4:161, 30:39 falls under the surplus/increase sense

claims.claim: In Q 3:130 'doubled and multiplied' is historically illustrative and descriptive, not definitional; the verse describes what people were doing rather than what ribā is.
premises: Q 2:279 supplies the legal definition: only principal is recoverable
A low rate can compound to multiples of principal, so size cannot mark the prohibition's boundary
Reading 3:130 as permitting small ribā contradicts 2:279 and violates 4:82's non-duality principle

claims.claim: The Qurʾān presents a universal, non-dualistic prohibition of ribā without in-group/out-group distinction, unlike Pentateuch, New Testament, and later legal-fiction accommodations.
premises: 2:275–279 categorically ban ribā as unjust consumption; 4:161 criticizes earlier communities
30:39 denies that ribā increases with God; only charity does
Murābaḥa-style markups equal principal plus time-based premium, a disguised interest charge

claims.claim: Modern global debt constitutes ribā as a structural extraction mechanism because money is created as principal only while debt carries interest, forcing perpetual expansion.
claims.source: Why Global Debt Outstanding is Ribā
premises: Global debt (~$345–346 trillion) exceeds broad money (~$140 trillion); interest is not created upfront
Paying principal extinguishes money; compounding claims outpace available money, requiring refinancing or crises
3:130's 'doubled and multiplied' describes this system-level compounding dynamic

argumentAudit.issue: Whether Q 3:130's phrase 'doubled and multiplied' (aḍʿāfan muḍāʿafah) defines the scope of the ribā prohibition or merely describes a historical manifestation of it, and whether any interest rate is permissible under the Qurʾān
disputed: Whether 'doubled and multiplied' restricts the prohibition to compound or excessive interest only
Whether a low or 'reasonable' interest rate is permissible under the Qurʾān
Whether trade markups (murābaḥa) and time-value justifications fall outside the ribā ban
notNecessarilyDisputed: Rejecting a definitional reading of 3:130 does not deny that compound doubling was historically practiced or condemned
Denying permissibility of any surplus does not assert that every credit transaction or deferred sale is ribā
Criticizing legal fictions does not claim the Qurʾān names specific modern instruments

The research's claim that the root ر-ب-و occurs exactly 20 times was not independently verifiable from the supplied corpus data (only the رِّبَوٰا lemma's 5 occurrences were supplied); the analysis reports the claim without confirming the count.
